newsitem.title: RUSSIA: No breakthrough for Germany's Kinkel in Russia.
newsitem.headline: No breakthrough for Germany's Kinkel in Russia.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus tried to soothe Russian leaders' concerns over NATO's eastward expansion plans on Wednesday, but emerged from a two-day visit to Moscow without any signs of breakthrough.

"Everyone I have met (in Moscow) has shown resistance to NATO enlargement," Kinkel said after meeting Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and speaking to President Boris Yeltsin by telephone.

Rodionov said Kinkel had brought no new ideas and that the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's plans to take in members of the former Soviet bloc showed a blatant disregard for Russian efforts to improve global security in recent years.

"I do not believe NATO is expanding in order to start a new war. But NATO is becoming...a powerful military alliance with which no one can now compare in terms of military might," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.
"We are concerned that NATO...coming close to the Russian borders, will try to dictate to us its political, economic and other conditions."

Russia says NATO's plans to take in new members from eastern and central Europe threaten its security, create divisions in Europe and undermine Yeltsin's authority. The dispute overshadows its whole relationship with the West.
Kinkel arrived in Moscow on Tuesday as part of an intense NATO campaign to reassure Russian leaders that the Western alliance's enlargement plans do not threaten Moscow.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini follows him to Moscow on Thursday. U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who has been touring European capitals, also starts talks in Moscow on Thursday which culminate in a meeting with Yeltsin on Friday.
She proposed in BrusseLs on Tuesday creating a joint Russian-NATO brigade, mainly for peacekeeping purposes, to try to reassure Moscow over the enlargement plans.
Primakov told Reuters after meeting Kinkel he had heard about the proposal through the media and declined comment.
But Deputy Foreign Minister Nikolai Afanasyevsky told Interfax Russia hoped Albright would outline her proposals during her talks in Moscow.
"This would be of interest to us," Afanasyevsky said.

Despite his lack of progress, Kinkel hoped that an agreement could be reached with Russia before a NATO summit in Madrid in July which is expected to issue membership invitations to Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic.
"We have to find a solution which allows us to have a successful summit in Madrid for all of us," Kinkel said, making clear he hoped Russia's concerns would be addressed.
Moscow appears to be seeking as many concessions as possible before NATO enlargement goes ahead.
Yeltsin, who is still recovering from pneumonia, reiterated demands for a legally-binding document setting out relations with NATO during his 15-minute telephone talk with Kinkel.
Moscow, which regards Germany as its prime ally in NATO, has said in the past that such a document must give Russia a say in decisions touching on its security interests.
Yeltsin also reiterated demands for Russia to be granted full membership of the Group of Seven industrial countries.
He has long asked the G7 to allow Russia into a fully-fledged Group of Eight, despite doubts by some of members that Russia was economically strong enough.
The G7 groups Germany, France, Japan, Canada, Britain, the United States and Italy.
